title: Minimum Window Substring — expand/shrink with frequency map + matched count.
shortTitle: Minimum Window Substring — Expand/Shrink With Frequency Map + Matched Count

s1_definition.profdef: Minimum Window Substring finds the shortest substring of a text that contains all characters of a pattern including their required multiplicities. A variable-size sliding window expands the right edge until the window satisfies all requirements, then shrinks the left edge as far as possible while still satisfying them, recording the smallest valid window. A need map plus a matched counter make each step constant, giving O(n) time.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India must find the shortest slice of a long log that contains every required event code at least as many times as specified. Rajesh extends the slice to the right until it covers all required codes, then trims the left as much as possible while still covering them, remembering the tightest slice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Expand until the window has everything required, then shrink from the left while it still does, tracking the minimum window.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Minimum Window Substring finds the shortest substring of a text that contains all characters of a pattern including their required multiplicities. A variable-size sliding window expands the right edge until the window satisfies all requirements, then shrinks the left edge as far as possible while still satisfying them, recording the smallest valid window. A need map plus a matched counter make each step constant, giving O(n) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India must find the shortest slice of a long log that contains every required event code at least as many times as specified. Rajesh extends the slice to the right until it covers all required codes, then trims the left as much as possible while still covering them, remembering the tightest slice.

**One line to remember:** Expand until the window has everything required, then shrink from the left while it still does, tracking the minimum window.

sections.s2_technical:
Build a `need` map of required character counts from the pattern, and track `required = need.size()` distinct characters that must be fully satisfied. Use a `window` map, a `formed` counter of how many distinct characters currently meet their required count, `left = 0`, and best bounds. For each `right`, add the character to `window`; if its window count equals its need count, increment `formed`.

While `formed == required`, the window is valid: record it if smaller than the best seen, then shrink by removing the character at `left` from `window`; if that drops its window count below its need count, decrement `formed`, and advance `left`. A code snippet: `while (formed == required) { if (r - l + 1 < bestLen) { bestLen = r - l + 1; bestStart = l; } char lc = s.charAt(l); window.merge(lc, -1, Integer::sum); if (need.containsKey(lc) && window.get(lc) < need.get(lc)) formed--; l++; }`.

The matched-count idea is what keeps it linear. Instead of re-scanning the window each step to check coverage, `formed` tells you in O(1) whether all requirements are met, updated only when a character crosses its required threshold entering or leaving. This mirrors the matched-count trick in the anagram problem but handles multiplicities and a subset rather than an exact permutation.

A senior nuance is tracking `formed` against the number of distinct required characters, not the total pattern length, and only decrementing `formed` when a character's window count falls strictly below its need. Characters not in `need` are still added to the window map but never affect `formed`, so extra characters are allowed as long as all required ones are present. Returning the best start and length at the end reconstructs the substring.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India incident team has a long event-code log and a set of required codes with minimum counts that together indicate a specific failure pattern, and they want the shortest contiguous log slice that contains them all so they can zoom into the root cause. This is exactly how minimum-window-substring works — the tightest window covering all requirements.

Problem 2 — Logs are huge, so a matched-count window that runs in a single linear pass is required rather than checking every slice.

The code shows an `IncidentLogAnalyzer` with `minCoveringWindow`, a demo on an event-code string and a required pattern, and the shortest covering slice.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: text "ADOBECODEBANC", required "ABC". The need map is A 1, B 1, C 1, so required is 3.

Step 1: The right edge expands adding A, D, O, B, E, C. When C is added the window holds one A, one B, one C, so formed reaches 3 and the window "ADOBEC" is valid, length 6, recorded as best.

Step 2: Now shrink from the left. Removing A drops A below its requirement, so formed falls to 2 and the window is no longer valid; left advances to index 1. The window "DOBEC" lacks an A.

Step 3: The right edge continues: adding O, D, E, B keeps formed at 2 until another A is needed. Eventually the window grows to include a later A and the counts re-satisfy, making formed 3 again at a shorter span.

Step 4: As the text reaches "...BANC", the window can shrink to "BANC" which contains one B, one A, one C, length 4, smaller than 6, so best updates to "BANC".

Step 5: No shorter valid window exists, so the method returns "BANC", the shortest slice containing all required codes.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Shortest covering window: 'BANC'
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Window Substring finds the shortest slice of a text that contains every character of a pattern with its required multiplicity, and I solve it with a variable-size sliding window that expands then shrinks. I build a need map of required counts and track how many distinct required characters are fully satisfied with a counter I call formed. I grow the right edge, adding each character to a window map, and when a character's window count reaches its required count I increment formed. Once formed equals the number of distinct required characters, the window is valid, so I record it if it is the smallest so far and then shrink from the left as long as it stays valid.

The matched-count counter is what keeps this linear. Rather than re-scanning the whole window each step to check whether it still covers everything, formed answers that in constant time and only changes when a character crosses its required threshold on the way in or out. It is the same idea as the matched-count trick in the anagram problem, extended to handle multiplicities and the fact that I need a superset rather than an exact permutation.

The subtle points I emphasize are that formed is compared against the number of distinct required characters, not the total pattern length, that I only decrement formed when a character's count falls strictly below its requirement, and that characters not in the need map are still added to the window but never affect formed, which is how extra characters are tolerated.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the incident service. We had a long event-code log and a set of required codes with minimum counts that together signalled a specific failure, and the team wanted the shortest contiguous log slice containing them all so they could zoom straight to the root cause. Because the logs were huge, the single-pass matched-count window was essential. Explaining the expand-then-shrink structure, the formed counter, and the distinct-required details shows the interviewer I understand this hard problem thoroughly.
